qAndA.answer: When the filters are aligned, essentially, nothing changes, and the light transmission remains similar to using a single filter.
qAndA.question: What happens to the amount of light passing through when the two polarizing filters are aligned in the same direction?

qAndA.answer: The frames are red and white.
qAndA.question: What color are the frames holding the polarizing filters?

qAndA.answer: The narrator finds it "disturbing" because it defies classical intuition – the order in which the filters are placed shouldn't affect the overall light transmission, yet it does.
qAndA.question: Why does the narrator find the results with three filters "disturbing"?

qAndA.answer: The middle filter needs to be at a diagonal angle relative to the horizontal and vertical orientations of the other two filters.
qAndA.question: In the demonstration with three filters, what orientation does the middle filter need to be in to observe the unexpected light transmission?

qAndA.answer: The narrator begins with a neutral and explanatory tone, but as the demonstration progresses, particularly with the three-filter setup, his tone becomes increasingly curious and subtly perplexed by the unexpected results, hinting at the counterintuitive nature of the quantum effect.
qAndA.question: How does the narrator's tone change throughout the video?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Here I'm playing around a polarized light.
Sunlight is unpolarized, so it doesn't really matter what angle.
If two filters, and they're polarized in the same direction, then essentially nothing too interesting happens.
If the polarizers cross, then essentially light making it through one filter is horizontally polarized.
Then the next filter only lets through the light that's vertically polarized, so cumulatively nothing makes it through.
This is used to have adjustable filters in photography fairly often.
Now something really interesting starts to happen, and in fact a quantum effect begins to kick in if I ask three questions.
So surprisingly, the answer I get depends on the order that I ask the questions.
So if I have a horizontally, diagonally, and then vertically polarized,
I get a different answer than if I ask horizontal vertical or horizontal vertical vertical.
So in between, I actually get a lot more light transmission than you'd expect.
And this is an angular dependent sort of transmission.
So it has to be between the asking the horizontal and asking the vertical question that I ask this diagonal question.
And this is really a quantum effect.
So if I ask the photons the same questions in a different order, I actually get a different answer, which seems a little disturbing to me.

youtube_description:
Crossing two linearly polarizing light filters blocks the light.  But adding a third polarizing filter at a diagonal angle lets light through again, but only if the diagonal filter sits between the two crossed polarizers, not if it comes before or after them.

There's a good explanation of the physics here, where it's clear the filters actually interact with the photons instead of just passively reading their constant polarization.
http://alienryderflex.com/polarizer/

Because light is also made of photons, how exactly you can interpret what a filter does to a photon gets much less clear, and simple ideas like "A photon has a polarization" no longer match reality--the polarization you read depends on the filters you apply.  Paul Dirac used this exact experiment as an introductory example to quantum mechanical effects in his 1930 textbook "The Principles of Quantum Mechanics", excerpted here:   https://www.informationphilosopher.com/solutions/experiments/dirac_3-polarizers/

These are the linear polarizing filters I bought (back in 2015, hopefully still good!): 
   https://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B004X3XFHU/      
(Not an affiliate link, and I have no connection to this seller.)
